subsystems.name: Qubit chip
subsystems.role: the quantum processor itself — a few to a few hundred physical qubits on a chip or in a trap.
parts: superconducting transmons, trapped ions, photonic circuits or nuclear spins

subsystems.name: Environment
subsystems.role: keeps qubits isolated from heat and noise, which is what makes them fragile.
parts: or permanent magnet at room temperature (NMR)

subsystems.name: Control electronics
subsystems.role: generates the microwave and radio-frequency pulses that manipulate each qubit.

subsystems.name: Readout chain
subsystems.role: measures qubit states without disturbing them more than necessary.

subsystems.name: Classical host
subsystems.role: runs the compiler and error-mitigation software around the quantum core.

subsystems.name: Software stack and error correction
subsystems.role: turns an algorithm into pulses, and combines many noisy qubits into a few reliable ones.

buildSteps.title: Pick a qubit modality
buildSteps.detail: Superconducting circuits need deep cryogenics; photonic and NMR designs can work at room temperature but with different limits.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the chip
buildSteps.detail: Superconducting qubits are patterned by lithography on silicon or sapphire, with Josephson junctions defined by shadow evaporation or oxidation.

buildSteps.title: Package and cool
buildSteps.detail: The chip is mounted in a shielded enclosure and, for superconducting designs, wired into a dilution refrigerator that occupies most of the physical volume.

buildSteps.title: Build the control stack
buildSteps.detail: Room-temperature electronics generate shaped microwave pulses on dozens to hundreds of channels, synchronised to nanosecond precision.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Each qubit's frequency, pulse amplitudes and readout thresholds are tuned individually; this is repeated as hardware drifts.

buildSteps.title: Run circuits, mitigate errors
buildSteps.detail: Small algorithms run with statistical averaging and error mitigation; useful results need error-corrected logical qubits.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop into a product
buildSteps.detail: Shrink the control and cooling hardware, add the classical host and software, and the result is a desktop-sized demonstrator — a few qubits, useful mainly for teaching and experiments.

prerequisites.why: current devices are too noisy for long computations; two-qubit error rates of roughly 0.1–1% limit circuit depth.
logical qubits that get better as more physical qubits are added have been demonstrated, but only at small scale.
a dilution refrigerator is power-hungry and bulky, so a true desktop machine needs a different modality or much better cooling.
each qubit needs several control lines; wiring thousands of them inside a fridge is a hard engineering problem.

prerequisites.tech: Software that maps real problems to qubits
prerequisites.why: without compilers and error mitigation, the hardware is unusable by non-specialists.

pathway.milestone: few-qubit desktop teaching machines and cloud access to larger processors
pathway.unlocks: hands-on learning and algorithm testing without owning hardware.

pathway.milestone: compact control electronics and integrated cryostats
pathway.unlocks: smaller racks rather than whole rooms — a step toward a miniaturised system.

pathway.milestone: error-corrected logical qubits with practical algorithms
pathway.unlocks: genuine advantage for chemistry, materials and optimisation problems — but run as an accelerator, not a personal computer.
a desktop appliance that accelerates specific scientific workloads while the classical PC does everything else.
